01.note: Rav Yosef employed a planter whose job was to plant trees in his field. The planter died, leaving five sons-in-law to carry on the work. Rav Yosef reasoned that one man had answered for the work alone, but five would each rely on the others and cause him a loss, so he told them: take the value of the improvement you have made and leave, and if not, I will remove you without it. He backed his threat with a ruling that a dead planter's heirs may be removed without payment for the improvement, but the Gemara comments that this ruling is not correct.
01.why: The Gemara is gathering cases on when a planter or sharecropper who leaves a field is paid for the improvement he made; this one asks what happens when the planter dies and his heirs take over.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: Owner of the field, who wants to end the arrangement with his dead planter's heirs.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: Sage cited by Rav Yosef for the ruling that a dead planter's heirs may be removed without payment; some attribute it to Rav Huna or Rav Nahman.

terms.meaning: A worker hired to plant trees in someone else's field and tend them, paid with a share of what grows, much like a sharecropper.
The added value a worker's labor has brought to the field, such as trees he planted. The question is whether he is paid for it when he leaves.

02.note: Runya worked as a planter in Ravina's field. He caused a loss, and Ravina removed him. Runya went to Rava and complained about what Ravina had done to him. Rava said Ravina had acted properly. Runya protested that Ravina had never warned him first, and Rava answered that no warning was needed. The Gemara explains that Rava held that a children's teacher, a planter, a ritual slaughterer, a bloodletter and a town scribe are all treated as already warned, since any loss they cause cannot be undone.
02.why: The Gemara has been discussing a planter who causes a loss and whether he leaves with or without pay for his work; this case adds that he may be dismissed even without a prior warning.

people.name: Runya
people.about: Ravina's planter, dismissed after causing a loss.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: Owner of the field, who removed Runya.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage Runya appealed to, who upheld Ravina's action.

terms.meaning: A worker hired to plant and tend trees in someone else's field for a share of the yield.
Treated as if already warned, so that one may be fined or dismissed for a loss without any warning being given first.
A practitioner who drew blood from patients, a common medical treatment at the time.

03.note: Rabba bar Avuh found the prophet Elijah standing in a graveyard of gentiles and asked him two questions of law, which Elijah answered. Then he asked how Elijah, a priest, could stand in a graveyard; Elijah replied with a teaching of Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai that gentile graves do not make a person impure, and asked whether he had not studied it. Rabba bar Avuh said he could not master even four of the six orders of the Mishna, because earning a living pressed on him. Elijah led him into the Garden of Eden and told him to gather leaves in his cloak. Leaving, he heard a voice say that no one consumes his World-to-Come like Rabba bar Avuh, so he threw the leaves away. Still, his cloak kept their scent; he sold it for twelve thousand dinars and divided the money among his sons-in-law.
03.why: The Gemara has been debating whether a creditor must leave a poor debtor his basic needs, as is done for one who owes a pledged valuation to the Temple; Rabba bar Avuh puts that very question to Elijah, who answers that the two cases are linked.

people.name: Rabba bar Avuh
people.about: A Sage who meets Elijah, is too pressed for a living to study, and is shown the Garden of Eden.

people.name: Elijah
people.about: The prophet, a priest, who answers Rabba bar Avuh's questions and leads him into the Garden of Eden.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai
people.about: Sage whose teaching, quoted by Elijah, holds that gentile graves do not cause ritual impurity.

terms.meaning: Leaving a debtor whose property is being seized the bare necessities he needs to live, such as food, clothing and bedding.
A vow to give the Temple the fixed worth the Torah sets for a person. If the one who vowed is poor, the Torah lowers the amount according to what he can afford.
A portion of produce set aside for the priests, with a blessing recited when it is separated.
The reward of the righteous after this life. The voice means Rabba bar Avuh is spending that reward now, in this world.

04.note: A man said to another: I am selling you the vine that grows on top of this peach tree. Afterward the peach tree was uprooted, leaving the vine with nothing to grow on. The case came before Rabbi Hiyya, who told the seller he was obligated to put up a peach tree for the buyer to support the vine for as long as the vine lasts.
04.why: Rav Ashi has just explained that a landlord who rents out 'this upper story on top of this house' has tied the house to the rental; this case of a vine sold 'on top of this peach tree' is brought as a parallel.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: The Sage before whom the case came, who ruled that the seller must supply a new support.

people.name: Rabbi Yitzhak
people.about: Sage who reported the incident, as quoted by Ravin bar Rav Adda.

05.note: Rav Ashi saw cracks in the synagogue of his town, Mata Mehasya, and demolished it right away. He then brought his bed into the building site and did not take it out until the new synagogue was finished, down to the drainpipes on the roof.
05.why: Rav Hisda has ruled that one may not tear down a synagogue before building its replacement, for fear it will never be rebuilt; the Gemara says this does not apply when the old building has cracks, and Rav Ashi's case shows it.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: Sage who demolished his town's cracked synagogue and lived on the site until the new one was built.

06.note: Herod, a slave of the Hasmonean royal house, desired one of its girls. Hearing a Divine Voice say any slave who rebels now will succeed, he killed all his masters but spared her; she cried from a roof that she was the last Hasmonean and fell to her death. Since the Sages taught that a king must be a born Jew, he killed them all, sparing only Bava ben Buta, whose eyes he put out. Hiding his identity, Herod urged Bava ben Buta to curse 'this evil slave'; he refused, citing verses and his fear. Herod revealed himself and asked how to atone. Bava ben Buta told him to rebuild the Temple, sending to Rome by a messenger slow enough that the work would be done before an answer came. Rome replied that he was a slave, not a king.
06.why: The Gemara has asked how Bava ben Buta could advise Herod to tear down the Temple, when one may not demolish a synagogue before building another; it now tells the episode, and goes on to ask how he could advise a wicked ruler at all.

people.name: Herod
people.about: A slave of the Hasmonean house who killed his masters and the Sages and seized the throne.

people.name: Bava ben Buta
people.about: The one Sage Herod spared, blinded and kept as an adviser; he counsels Herod to rebuild the Temple.

terms.meaning: The Jewish royal family who ruled before Herod. The girl claims that anyone who says he descends from them is really a slave.
A voice from heaven heard announcing a message, in Aramaic and Hebrew called a 'daughter of a voice'.
The central sanctuary in Jerusalem, which Bava ben Buta calls 'the light of the world' and 'the eye of the world'.

07.note: Ronya's field was surrounded on all four sides by Ravina's fields, and Ravina fenced them in. He asked Ronya to pay his share of what the fences cost, then a share at a cheap price of reeds, then just a watchman's wage; each time Ronya refused. One day, when Ronya was harvesting dates, Ravina sent his sharecropper to take a cluster, and Ronya shouted at him. Ravina said this showed Ronya valued the protection: even a goat would have to be guarded against. Ronya said one need only chase a goat away; Ravina answered that it takes a man to do the chasing. They came before Rava, who told Ronya to satisfy Ravina with what he had agreed to accept, or else be judged by the stricter ruling of Rav Huna following Rabbi Yosei.
07.why: The Gemara has been debating when the owner of a field enclosed on all sides by a neighbor's fences must share their cost, as Rabbi Yosei and the first tanna disagree; Rava's ruling in this case applies that debate.

people.name: Ronya
people.about: Owner of a field enclosed by Ravina's fields, who refuses to pay toward the fences.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: Neighbor who fenced in his fields all around Ronya's and asks him to share the cost.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The judge, who pushes Ronya to settle on a watchman's wage.

terms.meaning: A worker who farms another person's land in return for a share of the crop.
A Sage of the Mishna whose view, as Rav Huna rules it, would make Ronya pay half of what the fences actually cost.

08.note: Two people lived in one building, one upstairs and one downstairs. The lower story began to sink until it was unfit to live in, and its owner asked the upstairs neighbor to rebuild the house with him. The upstairs neighbor said he was living comfortably. The downstairs owner offered to tear it down and rebuild it himself, and to rent the neighbor a place meanwhile; the neighbor said he did not want the bother, and told him to crawl in and out on his stomach. Rav Hama ruled that by law the upstairs neighbor may block the rebuilding. The Gemara adds that this holds only while the supporting beams are still more than ten handbreadths above the ground; once lower, the downstairs owner may say that space is his alone.
08.why: The Gemara has been working out what neighbors at different heights owe each other in building and keeping up the walls between them; this case asks whether the upper resident can be forced to let the shared building be rebuilt.

people.name: Rav Hama
people.about: Sage who ruled that the upstairs neighbor may lawfully prevent the rebuilding.

terms.meaning: A unit of length, the width of a hand, roughly 8 to 10 centimeters. Ten handbreadths is a common legal minimum height.

09.note: A man began building a wall right outside his neighbor's windows, and the neighbor complained that it would darken his house. The builder offered to seal the windows and open new ones higher up, then to rebuild the neighbor's wall down to the windows, then down to the ground, and finally to rebuild his whole house. Each time the neighbor objected that the work would weaken his wall or that a new wall would not hold in an old house, and finally that he would have no place to live; offered a rented place, he said he did not want the bother. Rav Hama ruled that by law the neighbor may prevent the wall from being built.
09.why: The Gemara asks why this case is needed, being almost the same as the upstairs neighbor who blocked a rebuilding; it answers that it teaches that one may object even if he uses the house only to store straw and wood.

people.name: Rav Hama
people.about: Sage who ruled that the neighbor may lawfully stop the wall.

10.note: Rabbi Yehuda Nesia made the Sages pay their share of the tax for the city wall. Reish Lakish objected that the Sages need no protection: the deeds of the righteous outnumber the sand, and if sand guards the shore against the sea, their deeds surely guard them. When Reish Lakish reported this to Rabbi Yohanan, Rabbi Yohanan asked why he had not quoted 'I am a wall and my breasts are like towers', and began to explain it; the explanation breaks off. In a second incident, Rav Nahman bar Rav Hisda made the Sages pay the poll tax, and Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak told him he had broken the Torah, the Prophets and the Writings, citing a verse from each that he read as freeing Torah scholars from taxes.
10.why: The Gemara has been discussing how a city's residents are made to pay for its wall and how the cost is shared; these incidents raise whether Torah scholars must pay, and Rav Yehuda then rules they are exempt from the cost of the city gates.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda Nesia
people.about: Leader who made the Sages pay the wall tax.

people.name: Reish Lakish
people.about: Sage who objected that the Sages need no protection.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: Sage to whom Reish Lakish reported, who suggests a better verse.

people.name: Rav Nahman bar Rav Hisda
people.about: Sage who made the Sages pay the poll tax.

people.name: Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak
people.about: Sage who told him he had transgressed all three parts of the Bible.

terms.meaning: An argument from a lesser case to a greater one: if something holds in the weaker case, it surely holds in the stronger.
A tax charged per person, a head tax, regardless of property.

terms.term: the Torah, the Prophets and the Writings
terms.meaning: The three parts of the Hebrew Bible: the Five Books of Moses, the prophetic books, and the remaining books such as Psalms and Ezra.

10.flag: Two separate incidents (the wall tax under Rabbi Yehuda Nesia, the poll tax under Rav Nahman bar Rav Hisda) are combined, and Rabbi Yohanan's explanation in the first breaks off mid-sentence.

11.note: During years of drought, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi opened his storehouses and announced that those learned in the Bible, Mishna, Talmud, law and lore could come in for food, but the unlearned could not. Rabbi Yonatan ben Amram pushed his way in and asked to be fed. Asked whether he had studied the Bible or Mishna, he said no, and asked to be fed as a dog or a raven is fed; Rabbi fed him. Afterward Rabbi sat in distress, saying woe to him for giving his bread to an ignoramus. His son, Rabbi Shimon, suggested it might be his own disciple Yonatan ben Amram, who never wanted to benefit from the honor due to Torah. They checked and found it was so, and Rabbi said: let everyone enter.
11.why: The Gemara has just ruled that Torah scholars are exempt from some city taxes because they need no protection; it adds this story of Rabbi favoring scholars, then ties it to his saying that suffering comes to the world only because of the unlearned.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called simply Rabbi; he opens his storehouses in a drought, at first to scholars only.

people.name: Rabbi Yonatan ben Amram
people.about: Rabbi's disciple, who hides his learning rather than benefit from it.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's son, who guesses who the visitor was.

terms.meaning: The first written collection of Jewish oral law, the core text that the Talmud discusses.
The stories, sayings and teachings of the Sages that are not law, as opposed to halakha, the law itself.
Here, a person without Torah learning.

12.note: A crown tax was imposed on the city of Tiberias. Its leaders asked Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi to make the Sages pay their share; he refused. They threatened to run away, and he told them to run. Half the city fled, and the authorities waived half the tax. The remaining half came with the same demand and threat, received the same answer, and all of them fled, leaving only one launderer. The whole tax was put on the launderer; he ran away too, and the tax was canceled. Rabbi said: you see that suffering comes to the world only because of the unlearned.
12.why: Rabbi has just been shown feeding only scholars in a drought; the Gemara says this fits his view that suffering comes only because of the unlearned, and tells the incident in which he drew that lesson.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called simply Rabbi; he refuses to make the Sages share the tax.

terms.meaning: A levy imposed on a city by the ruling authorities, here on Tiberias as a whole.
People without Torah learning, called 'ignoramuses' in the translation.

13.note: Rabba made the orphans of the house of bar Maryon pay toward a charity. Abaye objected with a teaching of Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda that charity is not imposed on orphans, not even to redeem captives. Rabba answered that he did it to raise the orphans' standing, so that people would honor them as generous givers.
13.why: The Gemara has been listing which city costs may be collected even from orphans, namely anything they benefit from; this case asks whether they may also be charged for charity.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: Sage who levied a charity contribution on the orphans of bar Maryon's household.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Rabba's student, who challenges the levy.

people.name: Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda
people.about: Sage whose teaching Abaye cites: no charity is imposed on orphans.

terms.meaning: Paying ransom to free Jews taken prisoner, one of the most pressing uses of community charity.

14.note: Two butchers agreed that if either worked on the other's assigned day, his animal's hide would be torn up. One of them worked on the other's day, and the other tore up the hide. They came before Rava, who made the one who tore it pay for it. Rav Yeimar bar Shelamya objected with a teaching that townspeople may fine those who break their rules, and Rava gave no answer. Rav Pappa said Rava was right to stay silent: townspeople may make such rules only where there is no important person in the town; where there is one, they need his approval.
14.why: The Gemara has cited a teaching on what a town's residents may decide for themselves, such as redirecting charity funds; Rav Yeimar's objection quotes the same teaching's power to fine, and this case sets its limit.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The judge, here also the town's important person, who ordered the butcher to pay for the torn hide.

people.name: Rav Yeimar bar Shelamya
people.about: Sage who objected to Rava's ruling.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: Sage who explained why Rava was right not to reply.

terms.meaning: A town's leading Torah authority, whose consent the residents need before their own rules take force.

15.note: Rav Ahadvoi bar Ami asked Rav Sheshet how we know that a leper makes people impure during the seven days he counts toward his purification. Rav Sheshet reasoned that since the leper makes his clothes impure, he makes people impure too. Rav Ahadvoi pushed back, and each time Rav Sheshet argued from another case, Rav Ahadvoi answered that a verse states that case outright, and he said it mockingly. Rav Sheshet was deeply hurt, and Rav Ahadvoi became mute and forgot his learning. His mother, once Rav Sheshet's nursemaid, came and wept before him; he ignored her until she said: look at these breasts from which you nursed. Then he prayed for mercy for Rav Ahadvoi, and he was healed. So Rav Ahadvoi was called the infant who perverted his mother's ways.
15.why: Rava has just quoted a teaching on charity from a Sage known only as the infant who perverted his mother's ways; the Gemara stops to explain the nickname, then returns to the leper question and to charity.

people.name: Rav Ahadvoi bar Ami
people.about: Sage who mocked Rav Sheshet and lost his speech and learning; called the infant who perverted his mother's ways.

people.name: Rav Sheshet
people.about: Sage who was mocked; he prays for Rav Ahadvoi after his mother pleads.

people.name: Rav Ahadvoi's mother
people.about: Rav Sheshet's former nursemaid, who pleads for her son.

terms.meaning: The seven days a person healed of the skin disease the Torah calls leprosy must count, partway through his purification, before bringing his offerings.
Ritually impure, a religious status that bars contact with holy things until one is purified; it is passed on by touch and other means.
One of the small creatures, such as certain rodents and lizards, whose carcass the Torah says makes a person impure.

16.note: Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai saw in a dream that his nephews were destined to lose seven hundred dinars that year. Without telling them why, he pressed them to give to charity, and took money from them for it, until only seventeen dinars of the seven hundred were left. On the eve of Yom Kippur, the government sent men who took those seventeen dinars. He told them not to fear further losses, since the seventeen were all that remained. Asked how he knew, he told them of his dream; asked why he had not told them, he said he wanted them to do the mitzva for its own sake.
16.why: Rabbi Yehuda son of Rabbi Shalom has just taught that a person's losses for the year are fixed at Rosh HaShana: if he merits, the money goes to charity, and if not, the government takes it. This story shows that teaching at work.

people.name: Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai
people.about: Sage who dreamt of his nephews' coming loss and steered their money into charity.

terms.meaning: A silver coin of the period.
Doing a commandment, here giving charity, purely because it is right, not for what one gains by it.
The Day of Atonement, the most solemn fast day of the Jewish year, ten days after Rosh HaShana.

17.note: Rabbi Abbahu says King Solomon was asked who is destined for the World-to-Come, and answered: those honored before the Elders. The Gemara illustrates with Yosef, son of Rabbi Yehoshua, who fell ill and fainted. When he recovered, his father asked what he had seen. Yosef said he saw an upside-down world, where the important of this world were below and the lowly above; his father said he had seen a clear world. Asked how the Torah scholars fared there, Yosef said they were as important there as here. He also heard it said there: happy is one who arrives with his learning in hand, and no one can stand in the section of those executed by the government. The Gemara asks who these were, and says not Rabbi Akiva and his colleagues, who would be great anyway, but martyrs like those of Lod.
17.why: The Gemara is running through Rabbi Abbahu's sayings about charity and its rewards; this one turns to who earns the World-to-Come, and Yosef's vision of scholars keeping their standing there bears out Solomon's answer.

people.name: Yosef, son of Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: Fainted during an illness and on waking described the world he had seen.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: Yosef's father, who asks what he saw and calls it a clear world.

people.name: Solomon
people.about: The king, asked in Rabbi Abbahu's report who is destined for the World-to-Come.

terms.meaning: The life after this one, where the righteous receive their reward.
People of the town of Lod who were killed for the sake of God's name; the Gemara says they were not Torah scholars.
Great Sages put to death by the Roman government.

18.note: Ifera Hurmiz, mother of King Shapur of Persia, sent four hundred dinars to Rabbi Ami, who refused them. She sent them to Rava, who accepted them for the sake of peace with the kingdom. When Rabbi Ami heard, he was angry, citing the verse 'When the boughs are withered, they shall be broken off', which he read to mean that a nation whose righteousness has dried up should not be helped to earn merit. The Gemara explains that Rava accepted for the sake of peace with the kingdom.
18.why: The Sages have been debating a verse saying the charity of the nations is a sin for them; this incident shows two Sages differing over whether to accept charity from a gentile queen, and the Gemara goes on to reconcile them.

people.name: Ifera Hurmiz
people.about: Mother of King Shapur of Persia, who sent money for charity.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: Sage who refused her gift and was angry that Rava accepted it.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Sage who accepted the gift for the sake of peace with the kingdom.

terms.meaning: Keeping good relations with the ruling government, here by not refusing a royal gift.

19.note: This is the close of the Gemara's account of a gift from the Persian queen mother to Rava, which Rabbi Ami had criticized. Rabbi Ami was angry only because the people who told him about it did not finish the report: they left out that Rava had given the money to the gentile poor, not to the Jewish poor.
19.why: The Gemara has asked why Rabbi Ami objected when Rava accepted the gift for the sake of peace with the kingdom; this line resolves the dispute by showing Rava had done what Rabbi Ami wanted.

people.name: Rav Ami
people.about: Also called Rabbi Ami; the Sage who was angry with Rava over the gift.

19.flag: The story segment is a single clause ending the Gemara's discussion of the Ifera Hurmiz gift (the previous story); it has no events of its own and cannot be followed alone.

20.note: Binyamin the righteous was in charge of the charity fund. In years of drought a woman came and begged him to feed her. He swore by the Temple service that the fund was empty. She said that if he did not feed her, a woman and her seven sons would die, so he fed her from his own money. Some time later he fell ill and was near death. The ministering angels said to God that He had taught that whoever saves one life in Israel is as if he saved a whole world; should Binyamin, who saved a woman and seven sons, die so young? At once his sentence was torn up, and a Sage taught that twenty-two years were added to his life.
20.why: The Gemara is gathering teachings on the power of charity; after the debate over gifts from gentile rulers, it turns to a Jewish charity officer whose giving saved his own life, and then to King Munbaz, who gave away his treasures in a drought.

people.name: Binyamin the righteous
people.about: Supervisor of the charity fund, who fed a starving family from his own money.

people.name: The Holy One, Blessed be He
people.about: God, to whom the angels plead for Binyamin's life.

terms.meaning: The worship once performed in the Temple in Jerusalem; Binyamin swears an oath by it.
The angels who serve before God in heaven.
